A1.notes.Q3: I support using academic data if it significantly helps, but I am wary of invasive behavioral tracking (Absalon) and sensitive demographic data unless strictly for fairness adjustments.
A1.notes.Q4: As an advisor, I need clear reasons to build trust with students. A 'black box' model is unacceptable because I cannot explain the intervention or justify it during a meeting.
A1.notes.Q5: I prioritize ensuring we don't miss vulnerable students in specific groups (high recall). A small drop in total reach is acceptable if it means equalizing support across marginalized demographics.
A1.notes.Q6: Generic emails often get ignored. A meeting invitation is best for building rapport, followed by a personalized note. Outreach should happen immediately when risks are detected.
A1.notes.Q7: For generic info, casting a wide net is okay. For personal outreach from an advisor, we must be more selective to avoid 'alert fatigue' and damaging trust with students who don't need help.
A1.Q8.1: We need strict safeguards ensuring data isn't used for punitive measures or disciplinary action later. Student consent and transparency about what data is tracked are crucial for acceptance.

A2.notes.Q3: Course data is essential for my role. I am wary of 'panopticon' tracking via Absalon, but see value in first-gen/financial data if strictly used to level the playing field.
A2.notes.Q4: Trust is paramount in advising. I cannot effectively support a student if I cannot explain why they were flagged or what specific factors triggered the alert.
A2.notes.Q5: As an advisor, missing students in need is worse than false positives. We must prioritize catching vulnerable groups, even if total efficiency drops slightly to ensure equity.
A2.notes.Q6: Generic emails are often ignored. A personalized message showing we see their specific situation builds trust and increases the likelihood of them accepting help.
A2.notes.Q7: With generic info, casting a wider net is okay to avoid stigma. For personalized outreach involving advisors, precision matters more due to high resource costs and student privacy.
A2.Q8.1: Students need clear opt-out mechanisms and must be informed that their data informs support decisions, ensuring transparency rather than hidden surveillance.

A3.notes.Q3: Course data is standard for advising. Absalon activity feels like surveillance unless the gain in reaching at-risk students is massive (large). Sensitive data should be used only if it directly improves fairness.
A3.notes.Q4: Trust is paramount in advising. I must be able to explain why a student was flagged. 'Black box' models are unacceptable as they hinder the therapeutic relationship and create defensiveness.
A3.notes.Q5: Fairness is critical; missing vulnerable groups perpetuates inequality. I can accept a modest drop in total identification to ensure no group is systematically overlooked or unfairly harassed.
A3.notes.Q6: A low-friction generic email allows students to opt-in without feeling accused. Immediate contact is vital, as difficulties often escalate quickly during the semester.
A3.notes.Q7: With a general email, false positives are less intrusive but still noisy. With personalized advice from me, I have limited capacity; every contact must be well-targeted to ensure quality support.
A3.Q8.1: The model should include an opt-out mechanism and clearly state data usage in the privacy policy. Students need agency over their own prediction status.

S1.notes.Q3: As a former dropout, I fear intrusive tracking (Absalon data). Grades are fair game for support; sensitive demographics feel like surveillance unless they directly protect vulnerable groups.
S1.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I'm flagged to trust the help offered. A black box might make me feel judged or targeted, reducing my willingness to engage with advisors.
S1.notes.Q5: Ensuring no group is overlooked is vital. Even if we miss a few total cases, I worry that marginalized students are disproportionately left behind by opaque systems.
S1.notes.Q6: A low-pressure email is best; direct calls feel invasive. Immediate contact is crucial because crises happen fast, and waiting until year-end might be too late.
S1.notes.Q7: For generic emails, better to over-reach than miss someone in need. For personalized advice, precision matters more so I don't feel the university has an unfair assumption about me.
S1.Q8.1: How long is data kept? Could being flagged permanently affect my record or future opportunities?

S2.notes.Q3: As an international student working part-time, I worry about 'Absalon' tracking feeling like surveillance of my study habits outside official requirements.
S2.notes.Q4: Trust is essential for me to accept help. If I don't understand why I was flagged, especially as an international student facing cultural differences, I might feel targeted or stigmatized.
S2.notes.Q5: Prioritizing finding students in need (recall) is crucial. International groups are often missed due to different academic backgrounds; missing us hurts more than bothering those who don't need help.
S2.notes.Q6: I prefer a low-pressure generic email first. As someone working part-time, unsolicited phone calls or meetings feel intrusive and stressful without my consent.
S2.notes.Q7: With a personalized message mentioning specific struggles, false positives are too embarrassing. Better to miss some than risk exposing private academic issues unnecessarily.
S2.Q8.1: Data should never be used for administrative penalties or visa scrutiny; this support tool must remain strictly separated from legal/immigration departments.

S3.notes.Q3: As a student with a disability, I want data that helps identify specific barriers like mine accepted immediately. Other sensitive data needs strict justification to avoid stigmatization.
S3.notes.Q4: I need to know why I am flagged to trust the system and access relevant support. A 'black box' approach feels intrusive and unhelpful without clear reasons.
S3.notes.Q5: It is vital that vulnerable groups like students with disabilities are not missed, even if it means slightly fewer total identifications overall.
S3.notes.Q6: Generic emails are easily ignored. I need a personalized invitation to talk, as my health issues fluctuate and require timely, specific support.
S3.notes.Q7: For generic info, casting a wider net is okay. But for personal contact from an advisor, it must be precise to avoid feeling judged or harassed unnecessarily.
S3.Q8.1: The system should explicitly include feedback on whether the identified student actually found the support helpful after intervention.

S4.notes.Q3: As a student with ADHD and prior dropout, I fear invasive data like login tracking (Absalon). Grades are fine; disability data is risky unless it directly improves fairness for students like me.
S4.notes.Q4: Trust is essential for outreach to work. If I don't know why I was flagged, especially with my ADHD history, I might reject the support or feel judged by a 'black box'.
S4.notes.Q5: Prioritizing equal recall is vital for marginalized groups. Missing students who need help (like those with disabilities) perpetuates inequality, even if overall numbers drop slightly.
S4.notes.Q6: Generic email is low-pressure; a voluntary meeting offers human support if I'm ready. Continuous contact ensures help arrives before it's too late, which matches my ADHD struggles with deadlines.
S4.notes.Q7: For generic emails, false positives are annoying but low cost. For personalized messages from an advisor, being wrong feels intrusive; a balance is needed to avoid stigma.
S4.Q8.1: The system must ensure that flagged students don't feel stigmatized or punished. With my ADHD and past dropout experience, I worry about how this data might affect future perceptions of me by faculty.

S5.notes.Q3: As an international student, I fear being flagged based on nationality or past struggles. Academic data is okay for support if accuracy improves significantly.
S5.notes.Q4: Transparency builds trust. I cannot accept a system where I don't know why I was flagged, especially as an outsider unsure of expectations.
S5.notes.Q5: It is vital that international or marginalized groups are not missed more often. Missing students in need is worse than false positives.
S5.notes.Q6: A non-intrusive email gives me agency to reach out if needed, rather than forcing a meeting or call which feels too invasive.
S5.notes.Q7: If the outreach is generic, I prefer fewer contacts to avoid spam. If personalized, it must be very accurate to justify the intrusion.
S5.Q8.1: I worry about how cultural differences in study habits might misinterpret my behavior as 'difficulty' rather than just adapting style.

S6.notes.Q3: As a non-native speaker who previously dropped out, I fear being flagged for 'low activity' (Absalon) when I am just processing slowly in Danish. Sensitive data like nationality should be strictly off-limits unless it directly helps fairness.
S6.notes.Q4: I need to know why I was flagged. If the system says 'you are at risk' without clear reasons, it feels like surveillance and creates anxiety rather than helping me solve my problems.
S6.notes.Q5: As an international student who dropped out before, I worry models miss people like us more often. We should accept identifying fewer total students if it means ensuring marginalized groups are not systematically overlooked.
S6.notes.Q6: I prefer a low-pressure generic email first. If I'm struggling, seeing specific details about my grades in an unsolicited message is embarrassing and might make me avoid seeking help.
S6.notes.Q7: For generic emails, balance is fine, but for personalized messages, being too selective is crucial. Being contacted personally when I'm actually doing okay feels invasive and could damage my trust in the advisor.
S6.Q8.1: A major concern is that students with language barriers might appear 'disengaged' digitally due to slower reading times or hesitation on forums, leading to false positives for international students like me.

S7.notes.Q3: As a dyslexic student, I fear being flagged incorrectly based on slow digital activity (Absalon) rather than ability. Disability data is only acceptable if it significantly improves support for neurodivergent students.
S7.notes.Q4: If I am flagged, I need to know why. If it's because of my dyslexia accommodations or specific study patterns, a 'black box' explanation feels discriminatory and unhelpful.
S7.notes.Q5: Prioritize identifying students in need (recall) equally across groups. Missing vulnerable minorities is worse than slightly lowering total accuracy, though I can only tolerate a very small drop.
S7.notes.Q6: A generic email is least intrusive and lets me seek help on my terms. Continuous contact feels like surveillance; twice a year offers periodic check-ins without pressure.
S7.notes.Q7: For generic info, some false positives are okay. But for personalized advice from an advisor regarding my specific situation, high precision is crucial to avoid stigma.
S7.Q8.1: The system must not use my disability status as a direct predictor of failure; it should recognize that my extra time or different study pace does not equal academic difficulty.

S8.notes.Q3: As a Faroese student who previously dropped out, I feel vulnerable to surveillance. Course data is acceptable, but monitoring Absalon activity feels invasive and creates anxiety. Sensitive data like race or nationality should never be used due to high privacy risks.
S8.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I am flagged. If the system is a 'black box', it erodes trust and feels like judgment without cause given my past dropout experience.
S8.notes.Q5: It is crucial that international students or first-gen students are not missed more often than others. I would accept identifying slightly fewer total students to ensure the support reaches marginalized groups equally.
S8.notes.Q6: A low-pressure generic email allows me to seek help privately if I need it, without the stigma of being summoned for a meeting immediately.
S8.notes.Q7: With personalized emails or meetings, false positives are intrusive and embarrassing. The system must be very certain before contacting me directly about my personal situation.
S8.Q8.1: Students need to know they can opt out of data collection for support prediction without penalty, ensuring true consent rather than forced participation due to fear of missing help.

S9.notes.Q3: As a student with health issues, tracking activity is surveillance. I fear sensitive data like disability status could be misused or stigmatize me.
S9.notes.Q4: I need to understand why I am flagged to trust the process. If I can't see the reasons, it feels arbitrary and threatening.
S9.notes.Q5: As an international student with a disability, unequal systems hurt marginalized groups most. Missing students like me is unacceptable.
S9.notes.Q6: A low-pressure email is best. Constant contact feels intrusive, and I prefer finding support on my own terms.
S9.notes.Q7: For generic emails, false alarms are annoying but okay. For personalized advice, accuracy is crucial to avoid unnecessary worry.
S9.Q8.1: The stigma of being flagged as 'at-risk' when dealing with invisible conditions like mental health needs careful handling.
